analysis.one_liner: Writes the 2024 federal limits on PFAS "forever chemicals" in drinking water into law.
analysis.headline: Fifteen House members — 14 Democrats and 1 Republican — back making the 2024 PFAS drinking water limits permanent law, but the bill has sat in committee with no vote since June 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the drinking water limits for PFAS "forever chemicals" that the EPA finalized in April 2024 and write them directly into federal law. Right now those limits exist only as a regulation, which a later administration can revise or repeal; a statute would lock them in unless Congress itself changes them. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has sat with no further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks tap water would get legally enforceable limits on six PFAS "forever chemicals" in their drinking water, since the 2024 EPA rule would become statute rather than an agency regulation that a future administration could weaken or undo. Communities near contaminated sites, including military and industrial areas, would gain the most.

how_it_helps.text: The bill gives the force and effect of law to the EPA's April 2024 PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation as it stood on June 25, 2024, setting enforceable limits on six PFAS chemicals in public drinking water.
Because a statute can only be changed by another act of Congress, codifying the rule protects it from being weakened or repealed by a future administration through the ordinary regulatory process.

analysis.who_pays: Water systems would bear the cost of testing and treatment to meet the limits, and those costs would largely be passed on to customers through water rates. PFAS manufacturers and heavy users would face a permanent legal standard their products are responsible for meeting.

drawbacks.text: Water systems would bear the cost of testing and treatment to meet the limits, and those costs would largely flow to customers through water bills, with smaller systems facing the steepest per-household burden.

The bill simply freezes the rule as it existed on June 25, 2024, giving regulators no flexibility to adjust deadlines or standards as compliance costs and new science come in; it is a blunt instrument by design.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is broad and durable: legally enforceable drinking water limits on toxic chemicals that persist in the body and the environment, protected from administrative repeal. The cost is real but ordinary for a drinking water standard — utilities must test and treat, and customers pay through rates, with small water systems facing the hardest economics. The bill's main design weakness is inflexibility: freezing the rule verbatim means Congress, not EPA scientists, would have to adjust it later. On balance, the public health gain outweighs the compliance cost, though the burden on small systems deserves attention.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in June 2025 and has not been scheduled for any hearing or vote since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on June 26, 2025 by Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick with Rep. Debbie Dingell and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Fifteen members cosponsored the bill: 14 of 217 House Democrats and 1 of 223 House Republicans.
The bill would give the force of law to the EPA's final PFAS National Primary Drinking Water Regulation as it stood on June 25, 2024.
No hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled since the bill was referred to committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, since nothing has happened beyond the referral. If the bill stays parked, water utilities and PFAS manufacturers are better off avoiding the treatment costs and permanent legal standard it would impose, while communities relying on the rule keep only the weaker protection of a regulation rather than a law.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to write the 2024 PFAS drinking water rule into law.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup since it was referred on June 26, 2025; the action history shows no activity after the referral.

against.name: PFAS chemical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Chemical manufacturers and their trade association have publicly opposed strict federal PFAS drinking water limits and backed efforts to reconsider the 2024 rule.

sides.party_line_note: The bill is bipartisan by design — a Republican from Pennsylvania and a Democrat from Michigan introduced it together, and its 15 cosponsors split 14 Democrats to 1 Republican — but no committee or floor vote has occurred to reveal how the parties would line up.

industries.note: The codified rule would permanently require drinking water limits on PFAS these companies made and disseminated, strengthening the legal foundation for liability and cleanup obligations. A statute is harder to undo than a regulation, so the industry has an interest in the rule staying changeable.

Water systems would have to test and treat to meet the PFAS limits, and many would pass those costs to customers through rates. Utilities generally prefer regulatory flexibility that a fixed statute removes, even though their customers are the people the rule protects.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has sat without action in the Energy and Commerce Committee since June 2025, and most bills referred to committee never reach a floor vote. With no scheduled hearing or markup, it is likely to die quietly at the end of this Congress unless the committee chair or party leadership decides to move it.
